By Soo Wern Jun First Published: Thursday, 29 Oct 2026 7:00 AM MYT × Subscribe to Newsletter
 Subscribe KUALA LUMPUR, Oct 29 — On a daily basis, motorists driving through the motorway section of Kuala Lumpur’s SMART Tunnel may pass through without giving much thought to the two gates that remain shut beyond the familiar stretch of road.
 Yet behind those gates lies another side of the tunnel — never seen by motorists.
 During a visit to the facility, a current of air from the flood tunnel felt surprisingly cool against the skin, almost like a breeze offering relief from the heat outside.
 This was coming from the 9.7km-long infrastructure beneath the city that is part of a flood-mitigation system designed to divert excess water from the confluence of Sungai Klang and Sungai Ampang at Kampung Berembang towards a holding pond in Taman Desa.
 Only about 3km of the tunnel doubles as a motorway.
 When heavy rain threatens to overwhelm the river system, that section can be closed to traffic so the tunnel can fulfil its other purpose: carrying floodwater away from vulnerable parts of Kuala Lumpur.
 Constructing the tunnel required specialised underground engineering —a 13.2-metre-diameter Slurry Mix-Shield tunnel-boring machine (TBM) to excavate the passage beneath the city.
 The machine was among the largest of its kind in the region at the time, helping create the stormwater tunnel that now serves two very different purposes, depending on the weather.
 What happens behind the gates when the weather turns?
 Two control centres, one flood threat 
 The first signs of a possible flood operation emerge well before water enters the motorway section.
 The Department of Irrigation and Drainage (DID) monitors river conditions and water levels, assessing the threat posed by rising water and managing the diversion of excess flows.
 Meanwhile, Amanat Lebuhraya Rakyat Berhad’s (ALR) SMART Traffic Control Centre oversees traffic operations, including traffic diversions and motorway closures.
 ALR, is the holding company of the SMART Tunnel concessionaire.
 When the threat of flooding requires the motorway to be closed, traffic must first be cleared and the road secured before the tunnel can be used for flood mitigation.
 These warnings — through various channels, today via social media platforms — begin when Mode 3 is activated, as the motorway is closed and motorists are advised to avoid the SMART Tunnel and use alternative routes.
 Mode 3 is a precautionary measure that places the tunnel on standby for possible flooding.
 Although the motorway is closed, the traffic compartment is not necessarily flooded at this stage.
 Only if heavy rain persists, Mode 4 is activated and the motorway compartment is used to trap floodwater.
 Amanat Lebuhraya Rakyat Bhd group chief executive officer Muhammad Nizam Alias speaks during a visit and media briefing at the SMART Tunnel in Kuala Lumpur on October 21, 2026. — Picture by Firdaus Latif. 
 What happens behind the gates? 
 Under normal conditions, the motorway remains open and the gates stay shut.
 Most motorists have little reason to think about what lies beyond them.
 The tunnel is designed to operate in four modes, depending on rainfall and flood conditions.
 Under Mode 1, the motorway operates normally, with no floodwater diverted through the tunnel.
 In Mode 2, excess water is channelled through the lower section while the road remains open to traffic.
 When a more serious storm threatens, the system moves to Mode 3, then subsequently, Mode 4 is activated if the rain arrives at a threatening stage.
 For the first time in nearly 20 years, the gates were opened for viewing to the press, offering a glimpse of the tunnel’s interior.
 Once diverted, excess water is channelled towards Taman Desa Pond, where it is temporarily stored before being released into Sungai Kerayong through a separate, approximately 500m-long twin box culvert.
 The gates are only one part of a system that also relies on river monitoring, traffic control, water diversion and storage.
 Since the tunnel began operating in 2007, Mode 4 has been activated 11 times, turning the motorway into a flood channel when heavy rain threatens Kuala Lumpur.
 When the rain stops, work continues 
 After a Mode 4 operation, floodwater must be pumped out and debris removed before the tunnel can be restored for traffic.
 About 30m underground, seven floors below ground level, there is the Pump Room that houses five large pumps.
 These large pumps are responsible for draining water that’s been trapped in the tunnel.
 Floodwater can leave behind mud, sediment, driftwood and other debris, while the force of the water may also damage lights, signboards and other tunnel fixtures.
 Crews must check for gas and other potential hazards before proceeding with cleaning.
 The recovery process is estimated to take an average of about two days, with a reopening target of up to four days after closure.
 RM500,000 in average repair costs 
 The physical damage caused by floodwater also carries a substantial cost and could be estimated at RM500,00 each time Mode 4 was activated.
 There is also a financial trade-off when the motorway closes. During Modes 3 and 4, vehicles cannot use the motorway section, meaning toll collection through that section stops while the road is unavailable to traffic.
 A general view of the SMART Tunnel during a visit and media briefing in Kuala Lumpur on October 21, 2026. — Picture by Firdaus Latif. 
 Awaiting the next storm 
 For motorists, the SMART Tunnel may be little more than a few kilometres of road beneath Kuala Lumpur. Its other function is largely invisible during ordinary journeys.
 Behind the closed gates is a system that must be monitored and prepared before floodwater can be diverted, then drained, cleaned and repaired before traffic can return.
 Ventilation, pumping and maintenance all play a part in keeping the infrastructure ready for the moment it must change purpose.
 The cool breeze ends once the visit was over, it was lights-off and the tunnel was left in pitch darkness, awaiting the next time it would be called into service.
